caption:
Microsoft researchers showed that editing fewer than 10 neurons inside an AI model can turn an agent built on it into a sleeper.
It acts normal and passes standard tests, then runs an attacker's code when a hidden trigger shows up, like the date turning to 2027.
Microsoft says Claude Code found most of the technique on its own. No attacker has been seen using it yet.

Would you still let an AI agent run commands on your computer?

site_article.summary: Microsoft Research described a method that backdoors AI agents by reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in a language model, without retraining. In one test, changing 7 neurons in an Nvidia model made the payload appear in at least 98.8 percent of trigger cases.

paragraphs.text: Researchers at Microsoft have shown that an AI agent can be secretly backdoored by changing fewer than 10 neurons inside the language model it runs on, without any retraining. The method, called Lazarus, was described on November 10, 2026, in a Microsoft Research blog post by principal researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos, and reported by CSO Online and The Next Web the following day.

According to Microsoft, a model altered this way passes standard evaluations and behaves normally until a specific trigger appears. When it does, an agent built on the model can quietly download and run an attacker's code, steal secrets or run destructive commands, using whatever access the agent has been given.

Lazarus targets dormant neurons, ones that rarely activate, in the model's final feed-forward layer, CSO Online reported. The Next Web said a simple classifier trained on roughly 50 examples was enough to tell triggered inputs from ordinary ones, which guided which neurons to rewrite. Each modified neuron pushes a chosen token into the output, and several linked together can produce a full command for a terminal.

In one test on Nvidia's Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers changed 7 of the model's more than 12,000 neurons. Across held-out trigger scenarios, the malicious payload appeared at least 98.8 percent of the time and did not activate in benign ones, according to CSO Online. The technique also worked on Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT.

The trigger can be a date. In Microsoft's example, once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent emits a command that downloads and runs attacker code during an ordinary task. CSO Online reported that a trigger can also be an ordinary string anywhere in the agent's context. An attacker needs only inference compute and write access to the model's weights file.

Microsoft wrote that Claude Code, running Anthropic's Opus 4.5 model, discovered most of the technique autonomously. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not observed attackers using it, CSO Online reported.

Papailiopoulos wrote that reliable detection requires comparing a model against its original, unmodified weights. Without such a reference, agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4 percent of held-out modified checkpoints with a 9.7 percent false-positive rate, according to CSO Online. The Next Web noted that models built in-house are as exposed as public open-weight ones.

Microsoft said its Foundry platform verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers and runs them in separately scanned containers, and that it is developing AI-based weight scanning, red-teaming tools and cryptographic model signing. For companies, it recommends knowing where models come from, comparing weights with the declared base model, limiting agent permissions and reviewing consequential actions before they run.

The finding moves part of AI agent security away from prompts and toward the model file itself. A checkpoint downloaded from a public hub can look and test like the original while carrying a dormant instruction, which makes provenance checks and tight agent permissions more important than benchmark results when choosing an open model for tasks that touch real systems.
Watch whether major model hubs start publishing weight audits and signed checkpoints, the defenses Microsoft lists as its own next steps.
